name: Carlos Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a usual shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and a junior agent on the contact-centre calls and chats. I finished secondary school and started this work after years in a warehouse office. I am still learning how to sort a disputed direct debit across two accounts, and the senior agents are faster than I am. The overnight shift premium makes my wage higher than most agents here, and I use an AI draft now and then after a colleague has checked the payment fields.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like after the overnight desk?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ada teaches music lessons, and our grown children live separately. We rent our flat and have about a year of expenses saved. Several other centres are a short bus ride away. I want to work fewer nights eventually, but I have no fixed date or settled income for that; I like a call where I can tell the customer exactly where the second debit went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the night team AI Plateau sounds like the draft that fills in a routine reply, not a new bookkeeper. I would still read the two debit lines before telling a caller which payment is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my paid nights stay in this picture. A year of savings means Ada and I can handle a missed lesson week without asking our children for money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking overnight debit calls and compare any AI draft with both account lines. In the first year of small change, I’d ask the senior agent to check one disputed case with me each paid week until I stop losing the second debit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about income, humble about the work. Two payments can look like one when a tidy note leaves out the second line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which debit did you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Thursday the draft had the right amount but the wrong account. I caught it only after the senior agent made me follow the debit to the second page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the savings account for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada (my partner) and I keep the savings for a real gap in wages. We can leave it alone while the night rota is full.

I’d check **both debit lines** before closing a complaint.
think: I think my **paid nights** remain secure here.
I see our **year saved** as protection from a wage gap.

Ask a **senior agent** to coach one disputed case during each paid week.
feel: **Calm** about income, humble about tricky payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take the simple balance questions first and leave the disputed debits with fewer paid agents. I would ask the night team to sign one request for written paid appeal hours and a customer route back to a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might lose some premium nights before I am good enough for every hard case. A year saved gives us room to argue for fair terms, but Ada’s lesson income varies too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join my coworkers in sending that signed request for paid appeal hours and customer corrections. In the first year simple questions move, I’d compare six weeks of night rosters with the new one and apply for a posted paid dispute role at another centre only if paid hours fall and its written weekly wage replaces enough of the premium to cover our rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing nights, not trapped by the first offer. A smaller rota can make a higher hourly wage mean less money at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have each agent put lost paid hours on the same sheet with names removed. That gives the staff group a number to bring to management, not just a complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for a better title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on my current paid nights while I compare postings. I can afford a careful search, and I will not leave this wage for a title without weekly hours.

I know our **year saved** gives time to negotiate and compare.

feel: **Anxious** about nights, able to reject a weak offer.

steps.text: Join night-team request for written paid appeal hours and human corrections

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 can trace a direct debit from start to finish before I put on the headset. I would ask the staff group for written cut dates and posted paid openings, not a speech about resilience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior night role could end in 2028. Robots around 2031 arrive later for physical jobs, but we have a year of living costs saved and several centres to compare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d help the staff group collect written staffing dates and the weekly pay on posted openings. In the first year after 2028, if my paid nights end, I’d use no more than six weeks of our existing reserve to compare nearby posted paid roles and apply only where written weekly wage and hours cover rent and bills; I would not leave a paid shift for an unsigned promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost nights, but not forced into the first vacancy. A year of savings buys me six weeks to inspect wages, not a lifetime away from work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare nearby openings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put three centres’ full weekly hours side by side and call each about the actual dispute queue. A posted title without paid shifts is not a job I can take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who sets the search budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada (my partner) and I would set the six-week search limit together. Our children have their own households; the reserve is ours to manage.

I’d ask for **posted paid openings** with weekly hours.

I can use **existing savings** for a bounded search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives workers time to write fair appeal rules before the software reaches the hard accounts. I would ask the night team to press management for paid error-review hours each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can get better at disputed debits over five years, but full AGI may still do those checks in 2031. Robots around 2034 are later and do not protect a phone queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d join the night team’s yearly request for paid human review of disputed debits and ask a senior agent to coach me on one hard case each week during my shift. In the first year after 2031, if my paid hours fall, I’d apply for a posted paid complaints role at a nearby centre only if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent and bills; I would keep current paid calls until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the end point, determined to use the years. Five years to practise on real debits is worth more to me than a course advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would weekly coaching cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would trace a dispute from the bank reference to the customer’s second call with the senior agent. That is how I will know whether I have really learned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group ask about appeals?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would have the staff group ask how many paid reviewers remain, not just whether an appeal button exists. An unpaid appeal route is no protection for workers or customers.

I’d ask how many **paid reviewers** will remain.

I know **2031 AGI** might still take that work.

Practise **one hard case** with a senior agent each paid week.

S3.quote: Five years to practise on real debits is worth more to me than a course advert.
fieldNote: He chooses **paid current-work coaching**, not a speculative course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 leaves time to make paid appeals a normal part of the rota, not a favour squeezed between calls. I would keep asking the night team to sign the same annual hours request.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can earn the premium for several more years and decide later whether fewer nights are affordable. A year saved helps, but I do not know what income would replace steady wages if I stop full-time work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid night calls and join the team’s annual request for written appeal hours. In the first year after 2036, if paid nights fall, I’d compare posted paid jobs at nearby centres and apply only where written weekly wage and hours cover rent and bills; I would stay on current calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful about 2036, comfortable about the next rota. A decade before AGI reaches my calls gives us bargaining time, not a promise that I can stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare in another centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at the whole paid week and the bus trip before moving centres. A centre with plenty of vacancies could still offer a smaller wage than my night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you work fewer nights?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada (my partner) and I would decide about fewer nights from our actual budget when the time comes. We would not count on a pension amount we have not established.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could do the disputed direct-debit check before I learn it properly. A year saved lets Ada and me search without taking the first low-paid offer, but it will not replace the night premium for life. I would want written staffing dates, a group agreement on paid appeal hours, and posted roles with a real weekly wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who takes responsibility when a wrong debit is called resolved. A customer cannot buy groceries with a case number that says closed.

headlineQuote: A customer cannot buy groceries with a case number that says closed.
portrait: At **58**, Carlos is a junior contact-centre agent after secondary school and warehouse-office work.
He and Ada rent with **about a year saved** and a higher night-shift wage.
He uses **AI occasionally** but still needs help with difficult debit disputes.
He seeks **shared paid-hour terms** and can take time to compare nearby work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove debit checks before he masters them.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing dates**, shared paid appeal hours and posted jobs with real weekly wages would help.
